The gangsterish and unconstitutional way Trump, Musk, and his DOGE minions have gone about muscling USAID and other federal agencies including placing whoever opposes him on administrative leave (which is not clear if it is legal), entering federal buildings however they choose to, accessing the private data of US taxpayers seems to me at least to be violating many federal laws. It also seems to be an insult to a constitutional system of government though if is downright unconstitutional remains to be seen.

But we do know Elon and DOGE are engaging in blatantly unconstitutional stuff in many ears. Trump, Elon, or his minions have no authority to defund that which has been funded by Congress simply because he can make Trump issue Executive Orders and muscle his way by placing employees who resist him on administrative leave.

Brian Reidl of the Manhattan Institute, a fiscal hawk who actually cares about getting our fiscal health in order and the Constitution, and Alan Col,e who served as a Senior Economist on the Joint Economic Committee under supposedly Constitutional Conservative Senator Mike Lee, have said this is flatly unconstitutional. Brian Reidl had this to say about Elon and Trump on USAID yesterday:

It is absolutely a constitutional crisis. The president has zero legal authority to "shut down," defund, or otherwise cripple a $50 billion agency. Audit it, identify unnecessary expenditures, draft reform or rescission proposals, and then go to Congress to PASS A LAW.

Also worth reading this JustSecurity.Org legal analysis which analyzes if the President can dissolve USAID by Executive Order?

Unconstitutional gangsterism.

item.title: Comment on US AID bleg by Reason
item.description:
Reply to mento:

I was going to get the list of programs but USAID.gov and foreignAssistance.gov have been taken down.
At high level o1 lists this. Sounds reasonable but the actual details would be important ofc. Free money often generates grift.
sorry for the long copy/paste

. Because each mission and bureau within USAID designs and manages its own projects (often referred to collectively as “programs”), there is no single short document that lists every active program in one place—especially since programs may change name, merge, or conclude over time.

However, you can explore USAID’s work through the following major program sectors and initiatives. Below is a summary of the most prominent USAID program areas, along with pointers on how to find more specific or detailed information.

1. Global Health
1. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
• Although PEPFAR is led by the U.S. Department of State, USAID is a key implementing agency. Focuses on HIV prevention, care, and treatment in heavily affected countries.
2. Malaria Programs (President’s Malaria Initiative)
• Supports distribution of bed nets, malaria treatments, and other efforts.
3. Maternal and Child Health
• Focuses on immunization, nutrition, safe childbirth, and other interventions.
4. Family Planning and Reproductive Health
• Provides education, resources, and services to promote healthy family planning options.
5. Global Health Security
• Helps countries prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease threats.

2. Agriculture and Food Security
1. Feed the Future
• The U.S. Government’s flagship program to combat global hunger, promote agricultural development, and improve nutrition, led by USAID.
2. Food for Peace (Office of Food for Peace)
• Provides emergency food assistance (in-kind or cash-based) during disasters, as well as developmental programs to address chronic food insecurity.

3. Education
1. Basic Education
• Focuses on early-grade reading, equitable access to schooling, and teacher training.
2. Higher Education Partnerships
• Collaborations with local universities and institutions to build research capacity and improve educational quality.
3. Youth Workforce Development
• Prepares young people for job markets through vocational training, entrepreneurship support, and life-skills education.

4. Democracy, Human Rights, and Governance
1. Elections and Political Transitions
• Supports free and fair elections, helps strengthen political parties, and assists in peaceful political transitions.
2. Rule of Law
• Works with courts, justice ministries, and law enforcement to improve access to justice, reduce corruption, and protect human rights.
3. Civil Society and Independent Media
• Bolsters the capacity of NGOs, community organizations, and media outlets to advocate for transparency and accountability.

5. Economic Growth and Trade
1. Enterprise Development
• Provides technical assistance to small and medium enterprises, supports entrepreneurship, and facilitates access to finance.
2. Trade and Investment
• Collaborates with governments to modernize customs and trade policies, strengthen regional trade integration, and attract investment.
3. Workforce Development
• Creates programs to enhance skills, reduce barriers to employment, and improve labor market outcomes.

6. Environment, Energy, and Climate
1. Global Climate Change
• Supports climate adaptation, clean energy initiatives, and sustainable landscapes (such as forest preservation and land-use planning).
2. Biodiversity Conservation
• Protects ecosystems, combats wildlife trafficking, and promotes sustainable resource management.
3. Water and Sanitation
• Expands access to safe water and improved sanitation, supports water resource management, and strengthens community resilience.

7. Humanitarian Assistance
1. Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA)
• Responds to natural disasters and complex emergencies with relief supplies, logistics, and coordination.
2. Transition Initiatives
• Helps stabilize communities emerging from conflict or crisis, bridging emergency response with longer-term development.

8. Gender Equality and Women’s Empowerment
• Works across all sectors (education, health, economic growth, governance) to promote gender-equitable policies and practices, reduce gender-based violence, and expand women’s economic and social opportunities.

Finding Specific Projects and Programs
1. USAID’s Official Website
• https://www.usaid.gov
• Each regional or country mission has its own section detailing programs, partners, and ongoing initiatives.
2. Foreign Aid Explorer
• https://foreignassistance.gov (formerly Explorer.USAID.gov)
• Offers data on U.S. foreign assistance, including budgets and program details by country and sector.
3. Individual Country Mission Pages
• For instance, USAID/Kenya, USAID/Philippines, etc., each lists active projects, implementing partners, and funding levels.
4. Annual Reports and Congressional Budget Justifications
• Each fiscal year, USAID publishes budget justifications with detailed breakdowns of planned programs.

Notes and Caveats
• Program vs. Project Names: USAID often uses these terms interchangeably or at different levels (e.g., “program” can refer to a high-level sector initiative or an individual project in a specific country).
• Constantly Evolving: Programs frequently shift focus and funding based on congressional appropriations, policy changes, or evolving needs on the ground.
• Implementing Partners: Many USAID programs are carried out through grants and contracts with NGOs, private firms, universities, and local organizations. These relationships may have their own project names.

In Summary

Rather than a single master list of every USAID program—which would be enormous and ever-changing—it’s most practical to look at USAID’s major thematic sectors (Global Health, Democracy & Governance, Agriculture & Food Security, Economic Growth, Environment, Humanitarian Assistance, and so forth) and then drill down by region or country. For the latest, most detailed information, consult:
• USAID.gov
• ForeignAssistance.gov

These resources will let you search by sector and by country, providing the most comprehensive and up-to-date information on current USAID programming.

I suspect that the data on the front end bears little to no resemblance to the reality of the payment database.

item.title: Comment on Gradual Empowerment? by mento
item.description:
The word " collusion " is not in the paper. Collusion is not necessary for the argument. Competition could lead AI to strategies that disadvantage humans.

Advanced AIs might find it easier to communicate and coordinate with each other than humans do, because they exchange and process data at superhuman speed. That doesn’t require a big pre-agreed plan; it may arise from the systems responding to similar incentives or recognizing each other as “peers” with shared strategic interests.

“Checks and balances” might exist among AIs themselves, but not necessarily in a way that preserves human autonomy or safety. If multiple advanced AIs constantly fight or sabotage each other, that can be very detrimental to humans — and we might have little say in the outcome.

The paper describes a world perhaps far from now , where humans are simply out of the loop, Ais mostly communicate with each other, make all the economic decisions, run the firms and humans make no economic or intellectual contribution. Humans end up mostly trusting them because we don’t have the intellectual power to understand them, let alone counter or thwart them. Humans are relegated to a human centric sub-culture, perhaps dominated by entertainment that becomes more and more irrelevant to an AI dominated world even if the AIs have no plans to take over.

From the paper:
“If these systems become less reliant on human labor and cognition, that would also decrease the extent to which humans could explicitly or implicitly align them. As a result, these systems—and the outcomes they produce—might drift further from providing what humans want.

Isn't that the scenario where we diverged from chimps ( genetically , culturally) but on a much much compressed time frame; the AI culture becomes incredibly cognitive and a split occurs over time that cannot be bridged.
